2.2.6.2-f13.accuracy_reason: The old plague rule 'cito, longe fuge, tarde redi' is correctly described.

2.2.6.2-f14.accuracy_reason: In Charmides 156b–157a, Socrates gives this teaching (eye, head, body, soul), which he credits to a Thracian physician of Zalmoxis. This fits the sidenote 'E graeco'.

2.2.6.2-f16.accuracy_reason: Plutarch's Consolatio ad Apollonium quotes PV 'ὀργῆς νοσούσης εἰσὶν ἰατροὶ λόγοι'. Editions number this line between 377 and 380; 378 is a common citation.

2.2.6.2-f21.accuracy_reason: Paeon was the healer of the gods. In Julian's letter to Maximus, the Alexander-and-Homer comparison comes before the Paeonian clause.

2.2.6.2-f24.accuracy_reason: Aen. 1.153 reads 'ille regit dictis animos et pectora mulcet', and Aen. 1.57 reads 'mollitque animos et temperat iras'. The note's hedge 'appears to' is appropriate.

2.2.6.2-f30.accuracy_reason: Seneca Ep. 10.1 reads 'Lugentem timentemque custodire solemus, ne solitudine male utatur'.

2.2.6.2-f42.accuracy_reason: Aphorisms 1.1 says the patient, the attendants and externals must also do their part. Burton's Latin is a loose version of it.
